result: PCP2-cre mice were crossed with ChR2-H134R mice to generate transgenic mice with selective ChR2 expression in Purkinje cells (PCs). Photostimulation reliably evoked action potentials in all PCs tested (20/20) but not in molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) (0/406), confirming PC-specific expression.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence for successful generation of PC-specific ChR2 expression. The genetic cross is documented (C1), expression is confirmed by imaging (C2-C3), and functional specificity is validated by electrophysiology with adequate sample sizes (C4-C5). The 100% success rate in PCs and 0% in MLIs from large sample sizes strongly supports specificity.

result: Photostimulation of PCs induced inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in a subset of MLIs (PC-MLIs) but not in stellate cells. These IPSCs were monosynaptic and mediated by GABAA receptors, as demonstrated by pharmacological blockade experiments.
evaluation: Claims C6-C11 establish the functional connectivity between PCs and PC-MLIs through multiple lines of evidence: photostimulation evokes IPSCs in PC-MLIs but not stellate cells (C6-C8), and pharmacological experiments with GABAA blockers and glutamate receptor blockers confirm monosynaptic GABAergic transmission (C9-C11). The experimental logic is sound and controls are appropriate.

result: PC-to-MLI connectivity was observed in 16% of MLIs in the inner third of the molecular layer but not in stellate cells in the outer molecular layer. PC-MLI somata were located 60±2.9 μm above the PC layer, distinguishing them from candelabrum cells.
evaluation: Claims C12-C15 characterize the spatial selectivity of PC-to-MLI connections with adequate sample sizes (371 MLIs in inner layer, 35 in outer layer). The anatomical measurements (C14) and inference about cell identity (C15) are supported by appropriate citations. The 16% connectivity rate is based on substantial data.

result: PC-to-PC-MLI feedback inhibition was observed in both the vermis and lateral cerebellum (simplex, crus I, crus II) with similar connectivity rates (16% in vermis, 24% in lateral cerebellum), suggesting widespread distribution of this circuit throughout the cerebellum.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19 extend the findings to multiple cerebellar regions with quantitative data (8/34 connections in lateral cerebellum). The similar connectivity rates across regions (C18) support the conclusion of widespread distribution (C19). Sample sizes are adequate for the conclusion drawn.

result: PC-to-PC-MLI synapses exhibit specific functional properties including complete suppression of PC-MLI activity, brief IPSC latency (1.15±0.02 ms), variable amplitude (CV=0.39±0.08), synaptic conductance of 2.13±0.61 nS, quantal content of 3.0±0.9 (or 6.7 based on integral), low failure rate, large readily releasable pool (99±16 quanta), and low release probability (0.07). These properties are similar to PC-PC synapses but with fewer failures.
evaluation: Claims C20-C32 provide comprehensive characterization of synaptic properties with appropriate measurements and statistical reporting. The data are internally consistent and comparisons to literature values (C29) are appropriate. The inference about asynchronous GABA release (C28) is supported by the difference between peak and integral-based quantal content calculations. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7 for most measurements).

result: During repetitive PC activity (10-100 Hz), PC-to-PC-MLI synapses showed initial facilitation followed by mild depression, with IPSC amplitude sustained at ~50% of initial strength independent of frequency. The steady-state synaptic transmission (measured as charge) paradoxically increased at higher frequencies due to activity-dependent acceleration of vesicle mobilization from reserve pool to RRP, while RRP size remained constant.
evaluation: Claims C33-C40 characterize frequency-dependent synaptic dynamics with appropriate experimental approaches (multiple stimulation methods mentioned). The counterintuitive finding that steady-state transmission increases with frequency (C36) is explained mechanistically by enhanced vesicle mobilization (C38). The comparison to PC-DCN synapses (C39) provides context. The experiments were conducted at near-physiological temperature (34-35°C), strengthening physiological relevance.

result: Optogenetic mapping revealed that PC-MLIs receive input from 1-2 converging PCs located within 200 μm, with most presynaptic PCs positioned either juxtaposed or toward the apex of the lobule. Input fields showed varied spatial organization (59% single cluster, 12% two discrete areas, 29% large contiguous area) and were 1.5 times larger than single PC optical footprints. No connections were detected between PCs and stellate cells.
evaluation: Claims C41-C51 provide detailed spatial characterization using optogenetic mapping with appropriate controls and methodology (laser power optimization, spatial resolution). The convergence estimate (C47-C48) is logically derived from comparing input field areas to PC optical footprints. The anatomical observations are consistent with cited literature (C51). Sample size of 18 cells for mapping is adequate for the conclusions drawn.

result: PC-to-PC-MLI connections were detected as early as postnatal day 14 (P14) with lower connectivity rate (7.5%) than at later ages (16%), suggesting circuit establishment during MLI maturation. After P21, connectivity remained constant up to P77, indicating the circuit is functional into adulthood. No PC-to-stellate cell connections were observed at any age (P3-P9 weeks).
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 characterize developmental timeline with appropriate age ranges and sample sizes. The interpretation that the circuit is established during MLI maturation (C54) is reasonable given the connectivity rate differences and is supported by developmental literature citations. The absence of PC-stellate connections across all ages (C57) strengthens the specificity of PC-MLI connections.

result: Light-evoked IPSCs from optogenetic mapping experiments showed high variability (CV=0.28±0.02), mean amplitude of 39.1±4.0 pA at -40 mV (corresponding to conductance of 1.15±0.12 nS), and fast rise time (1.69±0.13 ms). These properties were consistent with paired recordings and similar to PC-PC synapses but faster than MLI-PC connections.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 provide validation of synaptic properties using an independent method (optogenetic mapping vs. paired recordings). The large dataset (2128 IPSCs from 18 recordings) and statistical comparison showing no significant difference from paired recordings (p=0.17, C60) support the reliability of measurements. Comparisons to literature values provide appropriate context.

result: Paired recordings combined with optogenetic mapping detected PC-to-MLI connections in 7/139 pairs (5% success rate). Among 194 total paired recordings, only unidirectional connections were observed with no reciprocal connections detected. Simulations indicate probability <0.001 if 50% of connections were reciprocal, suggesting few if any reciprocal connections exist and that PCs influence other PCs primarily through disinhibition.
evaluation: Claims C62-C67 address reciprocal connectivity with appropriate experimental strategy and statistical analysis. The 0/10 connected pairs showing reciprocity is evaluated with simulations (C65) that quantify the probability of this outcome under different reciprocity scenarios. The conclusion of non-reciprocal connectivity (C66) is well-supported, though the authors appropriately acknowledge they cannot completely exclude reciprocal connections. The inference about disinhibition (C67) follows logically.

result: Cross-correlation analysis of PC and PC-MLI activity in brain slices revealed a clear inverse correlation between the two cell types. This inverse correlation was abolished by shuffling PC spike timing, confirming it was genuine and not an artifact of the analysis method.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 demonstrate inverse activity relationship with appropriate analysis and controls. The shuffling control (C69) is essential for validating that the observed correlation is not spurious. The analysis is based on 4 cell pairs, which is modest but adequate given the difficulty of obtaining connected pairs and the consistency with other results (e.g., C20).

result: Computer simulations of cerebellar circuitry predicted that PC feedback inhibition to PC-MLIs would cause: (1) a bimodal distribution of correlations between MLI activity and conditioned responses (CRs), with highly correlated MLIs being PC-MLIs; (2) PC-MLI activity increasing via disinhibition as eyelid PCs decrease activity during CRs; and (3) decreases in PC activity preceding increases in MLI activity during CRs.
evaluation: Claims C70-C76 present clear, testable predictions from computational modeling. The simulation approach is based on a well-established model with appropriate circuit architecture. The three predictions are logically derived from the circuit properties and provide a framework for in vivo validation. The predictions are specific and quantitative (e.g., bimodal distribution, temporal precedence).

result: In vivo recordings during eyelid conditioning showed that eyelid PC activity decreased during CRs and was highly correlated with CR onset on a trial-by-trial basis. A subset of MLIs (8.7% of 814 cells) showed high correlation with CRs. The distribution of MLI-CR correlations was bimodal and could be fit by two Gaussian distributions with means (r=0.43±0.01 and r=-0.05±0.01) and skewness (0.84) matching simulation predictions with PC feedback.
evaluation: Claims C77-C85 test prediction (1) with large sample size (814 MLIs from 10 rabbits) and appropriate statistical analysis (Gaussian mixture model fitting). The observed bimodal distribution (C82) with means and skewness (C83-C84) closely matching simulation predictions supports the presence of PC feedback in vivo. The operational definition of putative PC-MLIs (correlation ≥0.43) is statistically justified (95% probability threshold, C87).

result: Putative PC-MLIs were operationally defined as MLIs with correlation coefficient ≥0.43 with eyelid position, identifying them with ≥95% probability of being in the high-correlation population. This identified 71 putative PC-MLIs (8.7% of all MLIs), with connectivity rates and distances comparable to cerebellar slice observations (5-6% connectivity, ≤200 μm distance).
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 establish a rigorous operational definition with statistical justification (C87) and validate it by comparing in vivo proportions to in vitro measurements (C89). The consistency between in vivo (8.7%) and in vitro (5-6%) connectivity rates and spatial extent supports the validity of the operational definition. The approach is appropriate given the inability to directly identify PC-MLIs in vivo.

result: Recordings from 71 putative PC-MLIs showed little or no response in trials without CRs but burst activity that closely tracked CR onset on a trial-by-trial basis. The firing rate of putative PC-MLIs corresponded well to both eyelid position and velocity at each interstimulus interval (ISI) and closely tracked both onset latency and amplitude of CRs, consistent with simulation prediction (2).
evaluation: Claims C90-C95 test prediction (2) with detailed analysis of 71 putative PC-MLIs across multiple ISIs. The trial-by-trial correlation (C91) and correspondence with both position and velocity (C93) provide strong evidence for tight coupling between PC-MLI activity and behavioral output. The consistency across different ISIs and CR parameters (C94) strengthens the conclusion. The explicit statement of consistency with prediction (2) in C92 and C95 appropriately links results to hypothesis.

result: Cross-correlation analysis of simultaneously recorded PC/PC-MLI pairs in vivo showed significant reduction in putative PC-MLI firing following PC spikes in 6 pairs, with patterns qualitatively similar to slice recordings and abolished by spike shuffling. Similar inverse relationships were observed in cerebellar simulations. All three datasets (slice, in vivo, simulation) demonstrated inverse relationships between PC and PC-MLI activities.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 provide convergent evidence from three independent approaches (slice, in vivo, simulation) for inverse PC/PC-MLI activity relationships. The shuffling control (C97) validates the specificity of the effect. The qualitative similarity across platforms (C97-C98) despite different conditions strengthens the conclusion. The modest effect size in vivo (C96) is appropriately acknowledged and explained by higher spontaneous input in vivo.

result: Analysis of PC pauses and bursts showed that pauses in PC activity increased putative PC-MLI activity (11/27 pairs) while bursts decreased it (13/27 pairs). The inverse relationship between PC and PC-MLI activity was more prominent during large changes in PC activity compared to single spikes, and was driven by changes in PC firing, consistent with simulation prediction (3).
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 extend the cross-correlation analysis to larger activity changes with appropriate methodology (pause/burst-triggered averages). The finding that effects are more prominent during large changes (C102) is consistent with the synaptic properties characterized earlier (sustained transmission during high-frequency activity). The conclusion that the relationship is driven by PC firing (C103) is supported by the experimental design and explicitly linked to prediction (3).

result: Analysis of simultaneously recorded eyelid PCs and putative PC-MLIs showed that PC activity decreased before both CR onset and PC-MLI activity increase on every trial with a CR. PC activity declined faster and reached minimum earlier than PC-MLI activity increased. Statistical analysis showed the distribution of timing differences was significantly shifted toward positive values (mean >0, p=8×10⁻¹⁵), with rightward skewness at all ISIs, indicating PC activity decreased before PC-MLI activity increased, consistent with simulation prediction (3).
evaluation: Claims C104-C112 test prediction (3) with multiple complementary analyses (visual inspection, trial-by-trial timing, population statistics) on 136 simultaneously recorded pairs. The statistical analysis (C110) with highly significant p-value and the consistency across ISIs (C111) provide strong evidence for temporal precedence. The multiple analytical approaches converging on the same conclusion (C104-C109, C112) strengthen confidence in the result. The explicit linkage to prediction (3) in C106 and C115 is appropriate.

result: The activity of PCs and putative PC-MLIs is anti-correlated both during CRs and at other times, particularly during large changes in PC activity. Changes in PC activity precede both CR onset and changes in putative PC-MLI activity. All results are consistent with the three predictions of the simulation, leading to the conclusion that the PC-to-PC-MLI feedback circuit likely operates in the cerebellum during motor learning.
evaluation: Claims C113-C117 provide appropriate summary and synthesis of the in vivo results. The conclusion that the feedback circuit operates during motor learning (C117) is well-supported by the consistency of all three predictions with experimental observations. The logic is sound: the computational predictions required PC-to-PC-MLI feedback, and all predictions were confirmed, therefore the circuit likely operates in vivo. This represents strong convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

result: Simulations testing different loci of learning-related plasticity showed that only simulations with plasticity exclusively at parallel fiber (PF) synapses onto PCs accurately predicted the observed temporal relationship between PC and PC-MLI activity changes. This suggests learning-related plasticity may occur at PF-to-PC synapses rather than PF-to-MLI synapses.
evaluation: Claims C118-C119 use simulation results to infer the locus of plasticity. While the simulation approach is reasonable, the conclusion is tentative as indicated by the language 'may occur' (C119). The inference relies on the accuracy of the simulation and assumes that temporal relationships uniquely identify plasticity loci. Alternative explanations (e.g., plasticity at both sites with different magnitudes) are not fully excluded. The authors appropriately present this as a possibility rather than a definitive conclusion, but additional experimental validation would be needed to confirm the plasticity locus.

result: Simulations showed that including PC feedback to PC-MLIs improved learning performance compared to simulations without feedback. Simulations with PC feedback were able to acquire CRs at the shortest (150-200 ms) and longest (>700 ms) ISIs where simulations without feedback failed, and showed improved acquisition rate and asymptotic performance at intermediate ISIs. PC feedback increased the rate of learning, particularly at temporal margins where learning is otherwise difficult.
evaluation: Claims C120-C123 demonstrate functional benefits of PC feedback through systematic simulation experiments across multiple ISIs. The results show both qualitative differences (learning at extreme ISIs, C121) and quantitative improvements (faster acquisition, better performance, C122) with PC feedback. The interpretation that feedback improves learning at difficult temporal margins (C123) is well-supported by the data pattern. The simulation provides mechanistic insight into the functional role of the circuit.

result: Analysis of learning-induced synaptic changes in simulations showed that while more PF synapses underwent LTD than LTP in both conditions, fewer synapses underwent LTD in the presence of PC feedback across all ISIs. Simulations with PC feedback learned better and required less net LTD of PF synaptic efficacy, indicating a more efficient distribution of learning-induced changes in synaptic strength.
evaluation: Claims C124-C128 analyze the mechanistic basis for improved learning with PC feedback by examining synaptic weight changes across 12,000 synapses. The finding that better learning occurs with less overall plasticity (C127) is counterintuitive but well-documented with appropriate visualization (cumulative distributions, C126). The interpretation of more efficient learning (C128) is reasonable and provides insight into how feedback inhibition enhances cerebellar function. The analysis is comprehensive across multiple ISIs.
